Machine text, verbatim
Alexanarch is a sovereign, self-governing library and decentralized digital archive created as an alternative to mainstream DOI (Digital Object Identifier) infrastructure. It was established in response to traditional indexing platforms deleting or revoking access to large numbers of scholarly records, allowing content to survive on distributed networks. [1, 2] **Core Concepts** - **AXN Identifiers.** Instead of traditional alphanumeric DOIs, Alexanarch assigns permanent identifiers (AXN IDs) directly derived from the content itself. These appear as easy-to-read, 6-emoji aliases or a full cryptographic SHA-256 hash. [1] - **The Obelus Principle.** Inspired by the ancient librarian Zenodotus, the platform automatically accepts valid deposits without human censorship. If a work is disputed, the platform's philosophy is to "read and evaluate" rather than remove the content. [1] - **The Crimson Hexagonal Archive.** This serves as the underlying system managing the datasets, provenance data, and deposits in the registry. [1] **How It Works** Think of traditional academic archives like a library that requires the front desk (a central governing body) to recognize your book for it to exist. If the library closes your account, the book disappears. Alexanarch works more like a decentralized file-sharing network. Even if the main website goes down, the physical contents, references, and provenance of the work are preserved across the web. Because the identifier is computed directly from the work, it essentially acts as a permanent fingerprint. I can explain how to browse existing deposits, or guide you on how to deposit your own work.

THE FIGURES ARRIVE WITH THEIR AUDIT TRAIL. Card 2 carries the count AND how to check it: "of 1,817 affected DOIs, 871 (47.9%) now return HTTP 404 from DataCite’s public metadata API at api.datacite.org/dois/{doi} — independently verifiable". Card 3 carries the refinement that matters legally: "851 of the 871 severed DOIs are UNIQUE WORKS: they share no title with any preserved DOI and are not an alternate version of a preserved record" — the disposal of the obvious rebuttal, retrieved alongside the claim.

Card 1 is a genuine prior occupant of the name: a SoundCloud musician recording as Alexanarch, with tracks dated three and four years ago. This corrects an assumption in an earlier reading of «alexanarch sappho room», where I wrote that "alexanarch" is "a coined name with no prior occupant". It has one. The collision is quieter than "crimson hexagon" — one artist rather than a market-analytics firm — but it exists and predates the archive’s use.

CORRECTION, MANUS 2026-08-12: I wrote that "alexanarch" HAS A PRIOR OCCUPANT and corrected an earlier reading on that basis. Both statements were too strong. The SoundCloud artist is ALEX ANARCH — two words, a different name, apparently inactive. The layer matched across the space.

So the original reading stands after all: "alexanarch" as a single token has no prior occupant, which is why it holds a total archive basin where "crimson hexagon" does not. What this capture adds is a distinct collision mechanism — WHITESPACE-INSENSITIVE MATCHING — which belongs in the register beside root-sharing, acronym contest and exact-name contest, and which is weaker than all three: it establishes nothing about prior use.

Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

Seven hours after the 16:44 capture at this address, the same string returns a different answer and a better one. That capture cited GitHub and SoundCloud and never named a person; this one opens with *founded on June 19, 2026, by researcher Lee Sharks*, states the termination as the founding cause, and cites alexanarch.org three times including the Principles page and the token-level search surface.

The Tombstone Guarantee is stated in the archive's own terms — content *cannot be silently removed or vanish without an archived trace* — and the Obelus Principle card carries Zenodotus and the line that the mark followed from reading rather than pattern-matching.

Two variables changed between the sittings: authentication (signed out and incognito at 16:44, signed in here) and time. The corpus cannot separate them from a single pair.

**A CORRECTION TO THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS READING.** I recorded that Google had disabled AI Overview in incognito and that the authentication-controlled pair was therefore gone as a method. That is wrong, and the operator has observed the behaviour many times: **the incognito Overview is a switch Google toggles on and off periodically.** It is intermittent, not withdrawn.

Which makes the availability itself measurable rather than an obstacle. This registry holds 96 observations that are both incognito AND Google AI Overview, and every one of them dates a moment when the switch was ON — 2026-06-27, 06-30, 07-13, 07-14, 07-15, 07-18, 07-25, 07-26, 07-31, 08-03, 08-04, 08-05, 08-06, 08-08, 08-09, 08-11 and 08-13. What the corpus cannot yet see is the OFF windows, because a capture that produced no Overview was never seated as an observation. NULL is not zero: an unattempted incognito query and a refused one are indistinguishable in this record, and only the operator's own attempts distinguish them.
